shipped_promises_as_shipped.deactivation_ui_copy: "Deactivate account — This disables your account and signs you out everywhere. You will not be able to sign in again. Confirm your password to continue." (verbatim from /settings in Chromium)
shipped_promises_as_shipped.deactivation_what_it_actually_does: POST /auth/me/deactivate re-confirms the current password (204), sets users.is_active FALSE, does NOT stamp deleted_at, leaves the username intact, and revokes every session row. Login is then 403 'account is disabled'. VISIBILITY: the PROFILE goes to 404 for everyone including the instance owner, and the account leaves /search/accounts and its channel leaves /search/channels (both queries filter u.is_active). Everything else stays fully public: the channel page 200 with its video grid, the videos 200 by direct URL and IN THE ANONYMOUS FEED, thumbnails/HLS/original 200, and the account's comments still render with its username on them. Deactivation enqueues NO search event, so the account's videos stay searchable in vidra-search (2 hits before, 2 hits after).
shipped_promises_as_shipped.deactivation_which_token_dies_when: REFRESH tokens die instantly (every session row is revoked; POST /auth/refresh is 401 immediately). The already-issued 15-minute ACCESS JWT does NOT: requireAuth verifies the JWT alone and never re-reads the account. Proven route by route right after deactivation — GET /auth/me 401 (it loads the user), but PATCH /auth/me 200, GET /me/notifications 200, GET /me/conversations 200, POST /videos/{id}/save 204, GET /me/playlists 200, GET /me/export 200 and POST /channels/{handle}/videos 201. The database confirmed the writes: the deactivated account changed its own bio and created a video row.
shipped_promises_as_shipped.reactivation_path: ADMIN-ONLY. There is no self-service reactivation: login stays 403 while is_active is false, and the UI says so. The instance owner flips it back with PATCH /admin/users/{id} {"is_active": true}, exposed in the UI as a per-row Reactivate action in /admin/users (driven in Chromium). Everything returns: login 200, profile 200, the videos back in the feed, /search/accounts back to 1.
shipped_promises_as_shipped.deletion_ui_copy: "Delete account permanently — This permanently deletes your account. Your channels and videos are removed for good, your comments are replaced with anonymous “[deleted]” tombstones (replies to them are kept), and your playlists, follows, history, and settings are erased. This cannot be undone — if you might come back, use Deactivate above instead." (verbatim from /settings)
shipped_promises_as_shipped.deletion_what_it_actually_does: DELETE /auth/me re-confirms the password (204, 0.30s for this fixture). The users row is ANONYMISED, not removed: username -> deleted-<8 hex>, email -> deleted-<8 hex>@deleted.invalid, password hash cleared, display_name and bio emptied, is_active false, deleted_at stamped. Channels and videos are hard-deleted; per-user rows (ratings, saved, history, playlists, follows both directions, notification prefs, account_exports) are purged; sessions revoked; comments on OTHER people's videos become tombstones with an emptied body while the replies under them stay readable; a comment on the account's OWN video goes with the video.
shipped_promises_as_shipped.dm_retention: THE RECIPIENT KEEPS THEIR COPY. The conversation, the message rows and the E2EE ciphertext all survive the sender's deletion; only the sender's IDENTITY is anonymised. B's /messages list after E's deletion reads 'deleted-251d3f2e — Encrypted conversation', and B can still open the thread (200). Nothing in B's view names the deleted account.
shipped_promises_as_shipped.media_cleanup: SYNCHRONOUS AND BEST-EFFORT, INSIDE THE DELETE — there is no ledger and no GC gate on this path. account.Service.Delete collects every DB-recorded blob key for each video (original, renditions, thumbnail, storyboard + its VTT, captions) before the rows cascade, deletes each object, then deletes the whole HLS key prefix, then the channel avatar/banner, the account avatar/banner and the export archives. Failures are swallowed so cleanup can never abort the deletion. Nothing is scheduled for later: MEDIA_GC_ENABLED and the media-GC worker are not involved in an account delete at all.

SC5_media_cleanup.gating: Nothing is deferred to media GC or a purge ledger. The blobs are deleted synchronously inside the account delete, best-effort. This slice therefore proves PHYSICAL removal, not just scheduling.
SC5_media_cleanup.proof: Real transcoded media on local disk: 55 objects before, of which 37 belonged to the account under test (originals, 240p renditions, thumbnails, storyboards + VTT, the CMAF/HLS ladder, and the export archive). After the delete, ZERO objects on disk carry either video id or the account id, video_files and streaming_playlists rows are gone, and every media URL (thumbnail, HLS master, original download, storyboard) answers 404. SC6_wrong_actor_and_edges.wrong_actor: There is no route by which one user deletes another: DELETE /auth/me is self-scoped, and B's DELETE /admin/users/{A} is 403 (requireRole admin). An anonymous DELETE /auth/me is 401.
SC6_wrong_actor_and_edges.wrong_password: 403 'incorrect password' with NOTHING changed — is_active still true, deleted_at still null, username still the original, all three videos still owned. A missing password is 422 with the field error.
SC6_wrong_actor_and_edges.oauth_only_rule: An account with an empty password hash (the OAuth-only shape) cannot self-delete OR self-deactivate: 422 on an empty password, 403 on any non-empty one, and the account is untouched afterwards. bcrypt can never verify an empty hash, so ConfirmPassword always fails.
SC6_wrong_actor_and_edges.admin_delete: Exercised only as the 403 refusal for a non-admin. The admin variant's self-guard was not re-exercised here (it is covered by TestAdminDeleteUser).

findings_recorded_not_fixed: THE HEADLINE. requireAuth never re-checks the account, so for the rest of JWT_ACCESS_TTL (15 minutes by default) a DEACTIVATED or HARD-DELETED account's still-valid access token keeps writing on every route that does not itself load the user. Proven AFTER the hard delete: PATCH /auth/me 200, POST /videos/{id}/save 204, GET /me/playlists 200, POST /playlists 201, POST /channels 201, POST /me/export 200 — the deleted account created a channel, a playlist, a saved row and a FRESH DATA ARCHIVE OF ITSELF, all after its own tombstone was written, and a comment it posted in that window is live and untombstoned in the public thread under the handle deleted-<suffix>. The UI's 'signs you out everywhere' and the doc comment's 'its access tokens stop resolving' are both true only of refresh tokens and of the handful of routes that read the user row. Closing it is a design decision (a per-request account read, a revocation set, or session-bound access tokens), not a surgical diff, so it is recorded rather than patched.

Deactivation is a login switch, not a visibility switch. It hides the profile and drops the account from /search/accounts and /search/channels, but the channel page, the videos, the public feed, playback and the account's comments — with its username still on them — all stay public, and vidra-search keeps serving the videos because deactivation enqueues no search event at all (unlisted does). Whatever the intended product answer is, the UI copy does not describe this either way.

An instance owner can flip is_active back to true on a TOMBSTONED row from /admin/users (the row shows up in the Users list as 'deleted-<suffix>' with Reactivate and Delete actions). Doing so makes a public profile page for deleted-<suffix> answer 200 again; login still fails (the hash is cleared) and the account does not return to /search/accounts. Harmless as observed, but 'Reactivate' on a hard-deleted account is a control that should probably not exist.

Delivered video.upsert rows in core's search_outbox still carry a deleted account's owner_id and video titles until the search_event_retention_days prune; the erasure deliberately only takes payloads that name the user at the top level.

attempts_and_corrections: The lab directory still held the PREVIOUS slice's state.json, so the first seed run skipped the owner claim and every registration came back 403 owner_claim_required. Worse, the `rm -f a b out-*.json` that was meant to clear it aborted whole under zsh's nomatch, so the file survived a second time. Every phase now starts from an explicitly established state.

The login response key is `token`, not `access_token`; videos have no transcode_state column; the tables are notification_prefs and e2ee_messages, not notification_preferences and message_envelopes. Five harness guesses corrected against the live schema.

psql -At with a field separator drops TRAILING empty columns, so an assertion about the wiped display_name and bio crashed the post-delete driver on an IndexError AFTER the (one-shot) deletion had already run. Its remaining assertions were completed by a continuation driver using the access token state.json still held, and every query that reads a possibly-empty column now wraps it in '['||col||']'.

Two assertions were simply wrong about the shipped behaviour and are restated: a comment on the account's OWN video is not a missing tombstone (it goes with the video), and the string 'alice' left in a thread is other users' comment text, not an identity leak.
The frontend could not serve /settings from .next/standalone (a turbopack chunk 404) — recorded as an unrelated finding; the walkthrough uses `next start` against the same production build.

Playwright: the admin Users row button is only actionable at a wider viewport (it timed out at 1280x900 and works at 1440x1000), and the row's Reactivate control lives behind the row detail, not in the list.
The browser walkthrough is not idempotent — it deactivates its actor — so a re-run needs the owner to reactivate first. Recorded rather than worked around.

for_the_next_slice.what_remains_for_AUTH_05_to_flip: Only the criterion's 'email/password changes … with re-verification'. Deactivation, deletion with content, the search deletion hook, DM retention and media cleanup are now all closed on evidence, and profile/privacy plus the archive were closed by the previous slice. There is no password-change endpoint and no email-change flow anywhere in the product (proven by 23 route probes in that slice), so the row cannot flip until the owner either builds current-password-authenticated password change and email change with re-verification, or rewrites the register row's criterion to describe what Vidra ships (a mailbox-possession reset, and an address that is fixed at registration). That is a product decision, not an engineering gap.
for_the_next_slice.highest_value_follow_up: the post-deletion write window — a deleted account should not be able to create a channel or a fresh archive of itself for fifteen minutes
